newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: YEAREND - High-flying Portuguese shares to stay aloft.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - High-flying Portuguese shares to stay aloft.

text.p: Portugal's stock market, among the strongest in Europe over the past year, looks good for a repeat performance in 1997, analysts and traders say.
Lower interest rates, further privatisations and confidence in Portugal's chances of making the grade for the European Union's monetary union will combine to keep investors interested, they predict.
The main market index, the PSI-20 index of leading stocks, rose nearly 30 percent in 1995, more than Wall Street, and the fourth sharpest advance in Europe.
Despite last year's sharp price gains analysts said stocks had not matched the surge in bonds.

The drop in bond yields, as prices have risen, has opened up an earnings gap which should make shares increasingly attractive to domestic fund managers who have been traditionally underweight in shares.
"The (stock) market has been catching up with the very sharp fall in long-term (bond) yields. But according to our model, there is more to come," said Mari Vargas of Santander Investment in London.
"We remain very upbeat for 1997. The fundamentals point to a very robust performance," she said.

Elizabeth Rothfield of Lisbon brokers Midas concurred. She noted that the combined earnings and dividend yield for Portuguese stocks would be significantly above the projected return from the benchmark government 10-year bond next year.
She said that Midas was predicting an earnings yield of seven percent together with a gross dividend yield of 3.6 percent against the some seven percent the Portuguese long bond is currently paying.
"Domestic funds should move into the stock market because they are looking for an alternative investment (to bonds)," she said.
Analysts put the weighting of Portuguese investment funds in the stock market at a maximum of 15 percent, which is low when compared with levels common abroad.

Although the price/earnings ratio for Portugal could be considered fairly high at around 14 -- it is above the Spanish equivalent which is under 13, for example -- the figure needs to be put in context, analysts said.

Espirito Santo Research (ESR) noted in a recent report that the P/E was swollen by the decreasing market weighting, following a spate of takeovers, of Portuguese banks which have traditionally had low ratios.
The bank forecast an overall earnings per share (EPS) growth of 18 percent for the Portuguese market next year, a healthy rise even if down from this year's 33 percent.
But the ESR said that its forecast stripped out the pulp and paper sector because its swing from low or no earnings this year to profit next could be considered as a distortion of the overall figure.

Overall EPS growth would also be restrained by dilution following a series of capital calls particularly for banks which would result in a net decline in earnings per share in that sector of some two percent next year, it said.
Portuguese share prices took off in 1996, after a dull previous 12 months, as a series of attractively-priced privatisations and mounting confidence in the local economy swelled interest and volumes.
In the first 11 months of 1996, average daily volume was up 50 percent at some 36 billion escudos ($230 million) compared with the previous year.
The Socialist government is still only halfway through a major privatisation programme, with a stake in profitable electricity giant EDP among the assets on offer in 1997.
"As long as things are not ruined by external factors, we are looking for strong market growth in 1997," said Mark Howard of Lloyds Bank Fund Managers in Portugal.
-- Lisbon bureau 3511-3150035
